title: Living on blood thinners: bleeding, food, other medicines
what: These medicines stop the blood from clotting too easily and protect against blood clots. But bruises and bleeding come more easily, so it helps to know a few rules.
why: After a blood clot, with some heart rhythm problems, after a valve replacement, and in other conditions, as decided by your doctor.
duration: usually months or lifelong; some people need regular blood tests
tell_doctor: Tell every doctor and dentist that you take a blood thinner
Before any surgery, tooth removal, or joint injection
If bruises appear for no reason or your gums bleed
If you start a new medicine, herb, or supplement

prepare.title: Timing
prepare.text: Take it at the same time every day. Set a reminder.

prepare.title: Tests
prepare.text: If your doctor ordered a clotting test, have it on schedule.

prepare.title: Food
prepare.text: With some medicines, steady eating matters, for example green vegetables. Ask your doctor about yours.

prepare.title: Card
prepare.text: Carry a note or card saying you take a blood thinner.

bring: A list of all your medicines and supplements
Your clotting test results, if you have them
The card or note about your medicine
steps: Take your pill at the same time each day
Mark each dose in a calendar or app
If you miss one, check the leaflet or call your doctor, and do not take a double dose
Ask your doctor or pharmacist before any new medicine
Over-the-counter painkillers too: ask your doctor first
Shave with an electric razor and brush your teeth with a soft brush
feel: Bruises appear more easily, and small ones are usually not dangerous
Cuts bleed longer: press on them for 10 minutes
after: Do not stop or change the dose on your own, only your doctor can
Alcohol only in the amount your doctor allows
Be careful with sports where you can get hurt
red_flags: Blood in the urine, black stools, or vomiting blood: call emergency services
A severe headache, a weak arm or leg, or confused speech: call emergency services
A blow to the head, even if you feel fine: see a doctor the same day
A nosebleed or wound that will not stop in 15 to 20 minutes

faq.q: Can I take a painkiller for a headache?
faq.a: Not all of them. Some painkillers increase bleeding. Ask your doctor which one is safe for you.
Yes. Be sure to tell your dentist about your medicine beforehand. Your doctor decides whether to stop it.

reminders.text: Time for your blood thinner. Mark the dose.
